*Tantra* means a continuum (*prabandha*), consisting of the *phalatantra* (the tantra of the result), the *upāyatantra* (the tantra of the means), and the *hetutantra* (the tantra of the cause).
There are thus three types of *tantra*. Among these, the mind that is naturally luminous and without beginning or end is the *bodhicitta*; it is the cause, and its seed is the *hetu-tantra*.
Of what is it the seed? It is the seed of awakening (*bodhi*). Perfectly complete awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) is the fruit, because it is the unsurpassed fruit.
Furthermore, that is the purification characterized by the destruction of all adventitious obscurations of that very mind which is naturally luminous.
The meaning is that this is the *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas, the locus (*āśraya*) of the infinite Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*) comprised within the *sambhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*.
This very thing is the awakening (*bodhi*) of the Buddhas, the *dharmakāya*, the state of the Great Vajradhara.
Therefore, the means (*upāya*) is the practice (*sādhana*) for the complete accomplishment (*pariniṣpatti*) of that fruit.

Furthermore, that path of the bodhisattvas—which has been cultivated over three incalculable eons along with its auxiliary factors—is, in the Mantra Vehicle, the means (*upāya*) consisting of the path together with its auxiliaries in the form of the maṇḍala circle and so forth; it is a condensed form of this very same exceedingly great path to enlightenment, which accomplishes awakening more swiftly and more easily.
With reference to these causes, results, and means, there are continuous teachings which are, respectively, the *hetu-tantra*, the *phala-tantra*, or the *upāya-tantra*.
These three kinds of tantra shall now be explained.

subsequently, he creates them again, having cleared away those very faults by reviving them through the sounds of the great banner and bell.
To the question, "Since this [goddess] is renowned among the Guhyakas as being illusory in nature, what follows from that? he says: "Of the Guhyakas," and so forth.
The gods of the external Vajra family are called Guhyakas because they are slightly hidden. She is their mother (*mātṛ*), meaning "the progenitor.
For this reason, she is renowned and celebrated as Mahāmāyā.
The meaning is that by forming the suffix *na* from *mīña* and *māḍha*, it is as stated before.
It is the coarse category (*audārika-riga*).
[The terms] *abhāvāmśa* and *abhāvāṅga* [are used].
"Buddha-awakening" means the awakening of a Buddha. It is thought thus: [the suffix] -ana is used here, meaning "it is not a state of harming. By applying the vowel *i*, it becomes *mar* (mother).
Furthermore, because it is applied as a causal condition, it also leads [the mind];
therefore, it is intended to be called *māyā*.
*Sāsa*.

This is its outflow (*niṣyanda*); it is the outflow of that. It is its movement (*niṣpanda*); it is the movement of that. Regarding *māḍh*: it is intended that by applying the *māla* suffix to *ma*, and being drawn forth [thereby], it becomes *māyar*. *Samharati*, *samharate*.
Having made those who were seen faultless— that is, having rendered them free from hatred— [he] did not [omit].
The various enumerations (*paryāya*) are as follows: *mīño*... such is the state of being. Om!
This Vidyā who accomplishes the three worlds is the bestower of all desires; may she herself remain thus.
To address the question of what this does for practitioners, he says "trailokya" and so forth.
Because its intrinsic nature is unsurpassed gnosis (*jñāna*), it is a *vidyā*.
This *vidyā*, known as Mahāmāyā, accomplishes the three worlds for practitioners.
"All desires" refers to all intentions, such as the state of a *vidyādhara* and so forth; it "bestows" these preeminently.
This half-verse constitutes the summary (*uddeśa*). Its detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*) extends from [the beginning] up to the words "by which... through the knowledge of *yoga-māyā*."

By whichever knowledge (*vidyā*) one becomes a sovereign achiever (*sādhakeśvarī*), through that very knowledge, the gods, the lords of wealth (*dhanada*), the *gandharvas*, the *yakṣas*, the asuras, humans, and any *vidyādharas*, *kiṃnaras*, great serpents (*mahoraga*), *rākṣasas*, and *piśācas* will be accomplished for practitioners; they will be brought under control, and all elemental beings (*bhūta*), whether born from water or born from land, will be subdued here by this [knowledge].
The connection is as follows: "by merely being known" means that they are accomplished for practitioners by merely being performed.
To the question "What are those things that are accomplished?", he says "the deities," and so forth.
The gods, headed by Śakra;
the Dānavas, who possess great supernatural power like that of Pretas;
and the Gandharvas, headed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra—these are so designated because they exist together with Yakṣas and others.

"In the *sādhya*s" means that they become the objects to be accomplished for the practitioners (*sādhaka*s); "they are accomplished" means they become subject to control; "subjection" (*vaśyatva*) refers to the state of being subject to control.
"Beings" refers to sentient beings; those born in water, such as sea-monsters and the like,
and those born on land, such as tigers and the like.
Thus, the means for accomplishing the external triple world has been explained.

Now, in order to explain the means for accomplishing even the supramundane triple world, he says "prakṛti" and so forth: "The nature of phenomena is luminous clarity, primordially pure and stainless; through the expression of skillful means, from that arises the self-arisen wisdom endowed with the five [buddha] families. Here, by this half-verse, the causal tantra (*hetutantra*) is taught in brief.
By the phrase "of the self-arisen ones possessing the five gnoses" (svayambhūpañcajñāninām), the sequence of the *vidyā* is indicated;
[the meaning of] "of this very one," "of that very one," "by which," and so forth, refers to "whose," and so forth.
B: amends *yasyetādi* in a marginal note; nor dag gnod sbyin yakṣādibhiḥ is omitted.
To be brought under control; to be subdued; to be brought under one's power; "sādhanī" means that which accomplishes, "sādhanāni" means those things which accomplish.
By the first quarter of the verse, the Tantra of Fruition is indicated;
by the third, fifth, and sixth quarters, the Tantra of Means;
and "prakṛti" refers to one's own innate nature.
By that [light], they are luminous, having the nature of shining, meaning they are pre-eminently pure.
What, then, are these? He says: "phenomena" (*dharmāḥ*).
Because they maintain their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they are phenomena; the meaning is all things.
Furthermore, all those entities are mind-only (*cittamātra*), because they appear as various modes of the mind itself;
just as in a dream, mental factors (*caitasika*) appear in the form of houses, gardens, ponds, elephants, horses, humans, and so forth, yet these too are specific states of mind.
And it is said in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*: "This triple world is mind-only."
It is also stated in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*:
"Agitated by latent impressions" (*vāsanāluṭhitam*) means afflicted or corrupted by latent impressions.
[An objection is raised: "Granted that all phenomena are mind-only, but why are they luminous and radiant by their very nature? To this, he says: "Primordially," and so forth.
"From the beginning" (āditaḥ) means starting from the very first;
they are "pure" (śuddhāḥ) because of the absence of all veils and impurities,
and "unturbid" (anāvilāḥ) due to the absence of the latencies of defilement.
The word *hi* has the sense of "because":
because they are pure from the beginning, they are luminous by nature (*prakṛti-bhāsvara*); because they are unstained from the beginning, they are radiant by nature (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*).
[Objection: But while the stains (*mala*) and their latencies (*vāsanā*) exist, how can they be pure and unstained?
Therefore, because the stains are adventitious to that intrinsic nature—just as darkness, frost, smoke, clouds, and dust are to space—it is for this reason that [the mind] is luminous by nature.
If it were not so, there would be no enlightenment for anyone; for since the stains are of the very nature of the mind, they could not be exhausted as long as the mind exists.
Therefore, the natural luminosity of the mind is the cause of awakening (*bodhi*), and awakening is the fruit.
Furthermore, that awakening is the ultimate purification of the mental continuum through the destruction of all obscurations along with their latent predispositions (*savāsana*).
This very [purification] is the *dharmakāya*, because it is the body, the abode, and the support of those phenomena comprised within the *sambhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*.

Because they are luminous (*prabhāsvara*), having the nature of shining forth, and because they maintain their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-dhāraṇāt*)—since even mental factors (*caitasika*) are specific states of mind—and because they are free from the appearance of objects and from obscurations (*varaṇa*), they are pure from the beginning (*ādi-śuddha*). Being pure from the beginning, they are naturally luminous (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*). Therefore, they are "naturally luminous. [This purity is] accompanied by the removal of latent tendencies (*savāsana*) and is absolute (*ātyantikī*). In that regard, the Blessed Buddhas, being self-arisen (*svayambhuvaḥ*), become [Buddhas] through the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) by themselves alone, due to the exhaustion of all obscurations and through their uniqueness (*kaivalya*).

Because they manifest by their very own nature, the five types of knowledge of the [Buddhas] are: the mirror-like knowledge (*ādarśajñāna*), the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*), the discriminating knowledge (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), the knowledge of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), and the perfectly pure knowledge of the dharma-realm (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*). Among these, the mirror-like knowledge is stainless like a clear mirror, infinite, and eternal.

The basis for the three types of knowledge situated in the middle is the locus where the reflections of all other knowledges arise; by means of which arising of reflections, the Tathāgatas become seers of all phenomena in all their aspects.
The knowledge of equality is the knowledge that there is no distinction between oneself and all sentient beings, and it is always conjoined with great loving-kindness and great compassion.

The wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) is unimpeded regarding all objects of knowledge; it is the treasury of all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*); it displays all its own majestic manifestations within the circles of assemblies; and it rains down great showers of Dharma.

That wisdom by which the Tathāgatas, in all world-systems, perform the welfare of infinite sentient beings at every moment through infinite emanations of body, speech, and mind—that is their wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).

That gnosis by which the Tathāgatas perceive the utterly pure suchness of all phenomena— because they see only that [suchness] and because all stains of signs no longer appear at all— that is their knowledge of the utterly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*). Among these, the first three gnoses constitute the *sambhogakāya*,
and the fourth is the *nirmāṇakāya*.
They are so called because they are a single portion of the fivefold Dharmakāya and are self-arisen possessors of the five wisdoms; that is to say, they are Tathāgatas.
Their means, which result in those fruits, are proclaimed—that is, they are taught primarily.

"In that regard" means: although the cause—namely, the intrinsic luminosity (prakṛtiprabhāsvaratva)—exists, this result does not arise without skillful means (upāya), because if it did, it would follow that everyone would attain awakening from the very beginning, since the cause is beginningless.
Therefore, skillful means are extolled.

The three morsels of the union of the yoginīs are accomplished without exception, entirely, and without remainder; they sport through all illusions. Regarding the passage beginning with "ke ta ity āha yoginī," the term *yoginī* refers to the five ḍākinīs, and *yogamātā* refers to Mahāmāyā.
"Without remainder in the three realms" means that all of the three realms consists of other arisen families and family lords;
how so? Because these are included within the three vajra-realms, which are the secrets of the Tathāgatas.

How are these methods [effective]? Since the cause— the perfection characterized by the fitness for enlightenment— exists, through the cultivation of these very methods, such as recitation and so forth, along with their necessary equipment,
one swiftly attains enlightenment.

And when that [wisdom] has been attained, it is accomplished for practitioners by way of both the path and the fruit, because through these very [means] comprised within the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the three types of enlightenment are brought to others according to their capacity. By the mere realization of which, everything—both the remainder and the remainderless—is known; thus, this very triad of groups beginning with the *yoginīs* is "remainderless" because not even a single group is abandoned.
Because not even a single deity is abandoned,
why is that [practice] accomplished entirely, completely, and without remainder? Because everything is a magical manifestation.

All this [is attained] through the destruction of all obscurations by means of the three bodies (*kāyas*). Within the circles of the assembly, there is the stainless clarity of a mirror; the fourth is the *nirmāṇakāya*, which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, characterized by the great rain of Dharma. Because it is beginningless, it is distinct from other causes such as recitation and so forth; the meaning is that the triad of rays is dependent upon the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*) during both the stages of the path and the fruit. That which was previously indicated as "the achiever of the three worlds" has now been explained.
Having stolen [the power] from all the Buddhas, she acts as the supreme goddess, the goddess, the maiden, the practitioner, the sovereign of yoga, the vidyā, and likewise the illusionist.

Regarding that which was indicated as "the bestower of all desires," he speaks to explain it further, beginning with the words "She takes away" (*harate*) and so forth: she "takes away" (*harate*), meaning she draws [beings] toward herself, whether for her own sake or for the sake of others; "she enjoys the Buddhas" (*buddhān bhunkte*) means that having drawn them in, she enjoys them. She is the foremost of goddesses (*sura-grā*), the best of goddesses (*sura-śreṣṭā*). "Yogas" refers to meditative absorptions (*samādhi*); "mastery" (*aiśvarya*) over them is the power of control (*vasitva*) regarding entering into and emerging from them. She is the "Vidyā" (Knowledge), the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*). "Indra-jāla" (the net of Indra) refers to the manifestation of armies and the like, as well as making them visible or causing them to disappear, according to the circumstances.

For those who exist or do not exist, [the rites] are delusion, paralysis, expulsion, killing, and so forth; as well as subjugation (*vaśya*), summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), and the like; and even the power of moving through the sky. Furthermore, there are activities such as entering another’s house and invisibility; or, for those who cause extreme harm to the Three Jewels and so on, [the rites of] inducing delusion (*mohana*), fainting (*mūrchā*), paralyzing (*stambhana*), making motionless (*niṣpandīkaraṇa*), killing (*māraṇa*), and expulsion (*uccāṭana*)—that is, causing them to abandon their place—and by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [one includes] breaking the limbs, fever, seizure by *rākṣasa* spirits, and the like. One who has come under control is "subjugated" (*vaśya*).

In this context, however, the rite for subjugation (*vaśya*) is described as "subjugating" (*vaśya*). There are two types of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*): summoning by the feet and summoning by the body. The first occurs on the earth, the second in the sky; these three are the rites of subjugation and summoning. By the word "other's city" (*parapura*), entry into another's body is meant. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [practices such as] leaping over [distances] are included. These very activities, beginning with the "other's city," are the "tasks" (*kārya*); "disappearances" (*antardhāna*) refers to invisibility. [The results are] brilliance, stupor, and likewise the ability to travel underground.

The Vidyādhara Universal Monarch himself becomes deathless and ageless; through this yoga of illusory knowledge (*māyā-vidyā*), he becomes free from illness. By means of the forms of the mantra syllables, wherever one goes, he is revealed by all the Buddhas. The great illusion (*mahāmāyā*) of knowledge effects emanation, manifestation, and disappearance; according to the application, the yogi sports with the planets.

"Enmity" (*vidveṣa*) is the causing of mutual hatred even between those who are in love; "paralysis" (*jambhana*) is the rendering mute; "descent to the underworld" (*pātālagamana*) is the entry into a subterranean cave. A great *Vidyādhara* is one capable of both suppressing and favoring these states. Their "nature" (*tattva*) consists of three things: youthfulness, immortality, and freedom from disease—all of which are easily understood. Furthermore, the meaning of "freedom from disease" is also implied; the remainder is that all this, beginning with delusion (*mohana*), is performed by means of this *Yogamāyā-vidyā*. "Māyā" refers to the Great Māyā; "Vidyā" is indeed knowledge, the single flavor (*ekarasa*) of all Buddha-dharmas; "Yoga" is union, and this Yoga is the *Māyā-vidyā*. Regarding the half-verse beginning with "*Vidyādhara*" and so forth, it consists of seventeen syllables, while the portion beginning with "*Nirvyādhi*" consists of fourteen syllables. Among these rites for seizing all Buddha-dharmas and so forth, some applications are to be explained in this very tantra, while others are to be understood according to other tantras. It was stated that they are "known merely by the syllable *Om*," which means they are accomplished merely through practice. To demonstrate this practice, he says "the syllable" (*akṣara*) and so forth. "The syllable" refers to the mantra-syllable, the form of the mantra, or the form born of the mantra. "By that" means by means of the syllable and the form of the mantra. "They transform" (*vikurvanti*) means they sport with the accomplishments of ritual actions and so forth. "Yogins" are the practitioners. "By recitation and by meditation, by visualization and by meditative absorption"—through recitation, one becomes a *Vidyā*, performing the *Vidyā-siddhi*. How do they practice the syllable? He says: "they recite" and "they contemplate. Here, "recitation" (*pāṭha*) is the muttering (*jāpa*) with speech; "contemplation" (*cintā*) is the muttering with the mind.
He explains how they practice the mantra-form with the words "visualizing," and so forth.
"Visualizing" means they see [it] through a continuous mental consciousness; "with meditative concentration" means by means of a state of mind that remains fixed upon that object.
By the words "recited" (*pathita*) and so forth, he states the fruit of the practice as it is performed:
"recited" means the *vidyā* (spell) known as Mahāmāyā has been chanted; "she performs" means she effects all rites such as attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) and the like.
By the second occurrence of the word *vidyā*, wisdom consisting of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*) is expressed.
Furthermore, that perfection of the cultivation of the form— the clear vision of oneself in the aspect of one's own deity—

shall bring about accomplishment for the practitioner; it shall effect the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) and, by the force of the word "and," shall also accomplish ritual activities (*karma*).
The accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā-siddhi*) is the manifestation of one’s own self in the form of one’s chosen deity, visible both to oneself and to others.

Regarding the passage beginning with *vidyādhara* and so forth: "the fourteen-syllable" refers to the syllable that is fully understood, the syllable of the mantra, the form of the mantra, and the body born from the mantra; the meaning is "by means of those. Through the *vidyā* (knowledge), through the stability of consciousness, and through the state of being established, one's own self appears in the form of the chosen deity. Regarding the statement that it is visible there, he speaks of the ease of practice in the performance [of the rite], beginning with the word *na* ("not"), and so forth.
Here, in the instances of the word *na*, the phrase *kārayet* ("should cause to do") is understood; thus, the meaning is "one should not do," and so on.
The rule consists of bathing three times and changing clothes three times, and so forth; the austerity consists of consuming food such as vegetables and barley-gruel,
which is difficult to endure, and the vow is arduous.
This is the summary; its detailed explanation is as follows: the fast (upavāsa) is non-eating;
it is a restraint (saṃvara), and for even a householder of intense passion, it constitutes celibacy (brahmacarya).
The beneficial sensations are those born together with the five consciousnesses, which are pleasures;
those born together with the mental consciousness are joys.
By means of these, practitioners achieve accomplishment.
The *mahāḍākinī* consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*) or an external woman cultivated as having that form is *prajñā*;

the means (*upāya*) for her is approaching her—that is, enjoying her by means of one’s own self cultivated in the form of Śrī Heruka. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the five offerings and the five qualities of sensual pleasure are included; "with these always" means at every junction (*pratisandhyam*).

The Hero resides in the center of the navel; he is the secret sphere of activity of Gesar. [He is] the nature of mind and non-mind, the form of mind, primordial wisdom, and the object of knowledge. Regarding the question, "How indeed does one experience bliss and joy through skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*)?", it says "the navel" and so forth.
"Navel" refers to the navel-lotus;
that which resides in its center is asked about, and it is said to be the "Hero."
Due to his union with unsurpassed vigor, the hero is Vajrasattva.
To the question of in what vessel he resides therein, he says "in the pericarp," and so forth; that is, in the pericarp of the navel.

"Gūḍhagocara" means having a hidden range; "gūḍha" is that which is hidden, meaning concealment or protection, and "gocara" is the vessel for that purpose. The meaning is the union (sampuṭa) of the sun and the moon.

Having thus stated his station and receptacle, he describes his intrinsic nature with the words beginning "mind" (*citta*) and so forth; "mind" (*citta*) means consciousness (*vijñāna*), and these are single terms used for the sake of emphasis.
Just as one who subsists on water alone is called "water-eater," or one who subsists on air alone is called "air-eater," so too here,
because there is no object of perception existing apart from consciousness, the meaning of the term *citta* is that "the universe is mind-only.
Furthermore, even that mind is no-mind (*acitta*).
Why is it "mind"? Because of the absence of an object of apprehension.
Why is it "non-mind"? Because in the absence of an object of apprehension, there is also the absence of an apprehender;
for in the world, consciousness is well known as the apprehender.
In this context, consciousness (*vijñāna*) itself is the mind (*citta*);

therefore, it is called "mind-and-non-mind" (*cittācitta*). If it is "non-mind" because it is devoid of the characteristic of mind as a grasper (*grāhaka*), then by virtue of which characteristic of mind is it "mind"? It is "mind" because its nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*).
Volition (*cetanā*) is what is meant by manifestation (*khyāti*), illumination (*prakāśa*), appearance (*pratibhāsana*), clarity (*sphuṭatva*), and non-mediacy (*aparokṣatā*).

That which has this as its form is "of the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpa*). Because it is conjoined with the characteristic of mind (*citta*) by virtue of having the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatva*), it is called "mind" (*citta*); such is the meaning. Now, if all cognition (*vijñāna*) is indeed of this nature, what is the distinction of the hero's own-being (*vīrasvabhāva*)? To this he says: "Knowledge," and so forth.
One's own, innate form (*svarūpa*) consists of both knowledge (*jñāna*) and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*); this is a *dvandva* compound.
That which has for its very nature (*svarūpa*) such knowledge and the object of knowledge is "that whose nature is knowledge and the object of knowledge" (*jñānajñeyasvarūpaka*).
It is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because by means of it something is known, and it is called "the knowable" (*jñeya*) because it is known;
[this is so] because [objects] appear even though the two apprehenders do not exist.

Furthermore, that which does not exist due to verbal expression is not a real entity; therein, even the non-essential nature [of things] becomes an object of knowledge for the cognitions of ordinary beings, because they conceptualize it as an object of apprehension.
Even though the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender are both non-entities, they do not constitute the intrinsic nature of those cognitions.
Rather, it is superimposed by delusion;
for this very reason, it is called the cause of delusion because it is a deluded state of mind.
For those for whom the object of knowledge is without intrinsic nature, their cognition of that which lacks intrinsic nature also becomes without intrinsic nature—that is to say, it is delusion.
For indeed, by the power of delusion, that which is non-existent or a non-entity appears;
therefore, that [delusion] is also cognition, because it is the cause of the appearance.
Moreover, that delusion is the innate nature of the intellect, because adventitious stains are not its intrinsic form.
Therefore, although their cognition does not possess an intrinsic nature, the ultimate bodhicitta is essentially non-conceptual knowledge (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*),
for conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is delusion.

Therefore, because all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are absent therein, his cognition is his very own nature and not even an error; since all causes for conceptual proliferation have set there and do not appear, his object of knowledge is his very own nature, and not even non-existent things. By this half-verse, the characteristic of ultimate bodhicitta—being the nature of non-conceptual gnosis—is directly stated as the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the Hero.
Its nature as great bliss (*mahāsukha*), however, is stated by implication, because great bliss is co-emergent with non-conceptual gnosis (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*).

Thus it is said in the *Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī*: "Having become one whose intention is non-conceptual toward this True Dharma, O Son of the Conqueror, having transcended the difficult path of conceptualization, one gradually attains the state beyond conceptualization."
"Tranquil, immovable, supreme, self-controlled, equal to the unequaled—the Bodhisattva attains from that the non-conceptual bliss of a being. Thus it is said.
In these two verses, "non-conceptual intention" (*avikalpāśaya*) refers to a firm intention.
"In this true Dharma" (*saddharme 'smin*) refers to the Mahāyāna.
[The word *cetana* is rendered as *cetane* in manuscript K.]
“Consciousness” (*cetanā*) ... [up to]: because it is luminous, it is the form of the mind (*cittarūpa*); it is that which is called mind, appearance, experience, manifestation, and non-obscuration.

“Having the nature of the object of knowledge” (*jñeyasvarūpaka*): because this nature of the object of knowledge exists in this, it is designated as having the nature of the object of knowledge (*jñeyasvarūpaka*). “Of cognitions” (*jñānānām*): [omitted].
[Of the two non-existent things] T: omits.
[Because of being a deluded mind] T: omits; "because it is grasped as a sign through delusion, it is called a 'delusive sign'.
[That too] J: syāpi.
Therefore, that error as well is not their cognition...
[it is] a derangement of the intellect (*buddhiviplava*).
[It does not occur] with respect to non-entities (*avastuni*). [Note: K and C read *avastūnām*.]
Having gradually transcended that, he is called a "Son of the Victor" (*jinātmaja*), that is, a bodhisattva.
Conceptual construction itself is the fourfold difficult path; having transcended it,
one attains the non-conceptual— meaning that one reaches knowledge free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
From that very knowledge, one attains non-conceptual bliss;
it is tranquil because of the absence of afflictions,
and unshakable because of its non-retrogressibility.
It is supreme because it excels all worldly and supramundane pleasures.
It is sovereign because it brings [pleasure] under its control according to one's wish and for as long as one desires.
It is equal because it is identical to other pleasures in terms of the category of pleasure.

It is equal to these very four distinctions. I shall explain those two: the profound teaching of the Buddha. Having made the *āli* and *kāli* equal, they should be applied to that diagram. I shall speak of such a hero.
To the question "In which vehicle is this established?", he says: "In the teaching of the Buddha."
The meaning is that whatever vehicle leads one to become a Buddha, that is the Buddha’s teaching, the Mahāyāna.

[An objection: But has this not already been stated by the previous verse? Why then say, "I shall explain"? To this he says, "profound" (*gambhīra*). The meaning is: in the profound Mahāyāna, that is, the Mantrayāna.

Indeed, in the Mantra system, which is distinct from the method of the *pāramitās*, the form of the *mudrā* and the retinue of the *bodhicitta* are cultivated as means for achieving enlightenment more swiftly.
Yet that has not been explained until now; therefore, he says, "I shall explain it.
He explains that very point with the words beginning with "Ali-Kali" and so forth.
"A" here refers to the union of the sun and the moon.
"Employed" means joined for the purpose of restraint.
To the question "Where?", he says: "In the line."
From that very Virāj, the *raśmir ekā* (the single ray) has arisen through the subtle aperture in the center of the moon; it is indivisible, uncuttable, and as fine as a lotus fiber.
How is it employed?
Having made that very [Virāj] equal to *āli* and *kāli*—meaning that in which *āli* and *kāli* are equal—it is so described.
How are they [arranged] in that [necklace]?
Because they are strung together in that very [necklace] by means of a string of pearls (*muktāvalī*).
How are they equal?

One attains bliss in the Mantra system through the retinue (*paricchada*). When that row of vowels (*akārālī*) at the two ends is ignited by the fire of the passion of wisdom (*prajñārāga*), it emerges from the Hero (*vīra*); then it becomes this "flow-producer" (*srutikāriṇī*). For here, the meaning of "flow" (*sruti*) is expressed by the word *sravati*; thus, the meaning is "flow. Now, he asks: what flows in that flow? He says: "the nectar" (*amṛta*). It is called "nectar" because it is liberation, because it is indestructible, and because it is great bliss (*mahāsukha*). What is it like? He says: "in the form of a drop" (*bindurūpiṇam*). Its meaning is that the Hero is white in color and has the form of the drop of great bliss. How does it flow? He says: "in the form of semen" (*śukrarūpeṇa*). Because the essence of pure gnosis (*viśuddhajñānarasa*) is a liquid of white bliss, it is spoken of by the word "semen" due to its similarity to semen; it flows, it trickles, in that form—that is, it trickles. Thus, by the words "the row of consonants" (*ālikālī*) and so forth, the stability of the Hero is stated; by "ignited" and so forth, his activity (*karman*); by "nectar," his intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); and by "in the form of a drop," his seal-form (*mudrākāra*) is described. How, then, does this become his seal? It is said: That subtle drop, white as the moon, is the mind (*citta*), because it shines within. Furthermore, the abiding of the mind in those [subtle elements] alone is "mind-only" (*cittamātratā*), because no object separate from the mind is perceived. Because there is an absence of an object to be grasped (*grāhya*), there is a lack of a grasper (*agrāhakatā*); that is its state of non-mind (*acittatā*). Therefore, it is of the nature of emptiness (*śūnyarūpa*). Furthermore, its shining forth is its nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*). Moreover, the subsiding of all signs of conceptual proliferation for the mind abiding in that alone is its nature of knowledge and the known (*jñānajñeyarūpatā*). And this is the form of the subtle gnosis-seal (*jñānamudrā*) of this Vajradhara. It is also said in the *Śrī-samāja*: "One should meditate on the moon-maṇḍala situated in the middle of the space-element. Having visualized the image, one should begin the subtle yoga. One should contemplate a mustard seed at the tip of the nose; within the mustard seed, the moving and the unmoving. One should meditate on the delightful station of gnosis, the secret fashioned by gnosis."* *Note: The text provided contains a mix of Sanskrit and Tibetan terminology (e.g., *paricchada*, *akārālī*, *srutikāriṇī*, *bindurūpiṇam*, *śukrarūpeṇa*, *amṛtam*, *cittamātratā*, *acittatā*, *śūnyarūpa*, *cidrūpatā*, *jñānajñeyarūpatā*, *vajradharasya*, *jñānamudrākāra*, *śrīsamāje*). In the *Śrīvajrāmṛta* as well, this subtle yoga of his is taught as common [to all] along with its ritual application: "One should remain motionless and begin the meditation on the nectar of knowledge. One meditates upon the supreme reality, the nectar in the form of a drop (*bindu*), which shines like the moon in the midst of space; it is declared to be the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatattva*), imperishable, unchanging, subtle, the Vajrasattva, and the unstruck (*anāhata*). The deity resides in the center of the navel, hidden within the pericarp of the lotus; situated between the vulva and the penis, he flows in the form of semen. Thus it is said.

"Blissful white-colored" means blissful flow; this is what is expressed by the word *śukra*. It flows, and it flows like the moon-white [semen]. Its nature is consciousness (*cidrūpatā*), consisting of both knowledge and the object of knowledge. Therefore, as it is recited in that Tantra, such indeed is the yoga here, and not action. Furthermore, in these places, the four wheels (*cakras*) are to be meditated upon.

Nor is it the case that the *caṇḍālī*, having ignited and heated the four wheels (*cakra*), emerged and expanded, heated the four wheels of all the Buddhas, and then returned and entered the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukha-cakra*), causing the flow of nectar from the syllable *Haṃ*—all of which is seen and brought forward by some; for that is incorrect, because there is no authoritative statement (*vācaka*) for it, and because the various tantras have diverse modes of realization (*abhisamaya*), whereas this tantra has an extremely concise mode of realization.
Therefore, one should touch upon each [wheel] as being composed of all the Buddhas and determine it to be the individual nature of every Buddha without exception.
How is it that [the mind] is by its very nature composed of all Buddhas?
It means "by its own nature" or "by its primordial essence.
For thus the dharmadhātu, which is without beginning or end, is the primordial nature of all phenomena.

And that very *dharmadhātu* is the supreme form (*paramaṃ rūpaṃ*) of all Buddhas; therefore, by that intrinsic nature (*svabhāvena*), it consists of all Buddhas. Not only by its intrinsic nature, but also by being supremely infused (*paramāhita-yogena*), it is called the supreme, supramundane (*lokottara*) knowledge—non-conceptual (*niṣprapañca*) and termed "Hero" (*vīra*).

By this [knowledge], there is the accomplishment of what has been infused (*āhitasādhana*), meaning the state of being produced (*janitatva*); the sense is that it is the outflow (*nisyanda*) of the Hero, which is the supreme infusion.

In that context, "yoga" means resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*). Through that, whatever appears as an object of vision and so forth—such as the visible and so on—is seen by the Hero alone. Because it is the state of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), by the phrase "because it is the state of clear realization," and so on, its nature as an object is perceived: one should see, smell, taste, and touch each and every thing as consisting of all Buddhas; one should ascertain that very thing as being composed of all Buddhas. By that intrinsic nature, each and every thing consists of all Buddhas; and if it is the outflow (*nisyanda*) of the Hero, then yoga is the appearance [of things] through resolute conviction—this is the meaning.
Will the accomplishment of the great *samaya* and the practice of the great pill (*mahā-guṭikā*) also perform the application of the vows of the great *māyā* ritual?
[The text] states another ritual action beginning with "The mandala lord is the great *samaya*," and so forth;
the *samaya* is the deity.
The "great assembly" (mahāsamaya) refers to its accomplishment (siddhi), that is, its fulfillment; the word "tu" is for the purpose of completing the meter.
That accomplishment is the great pill-attainment (*mahāgulikāsādhana*);
the drop of gnosis (*jñānabindu*) is the pill,

By means of that, there is the accomplishment of wealth, the success of the Great Pledge (*mahāsamaya*).

the Lord of the Mandala is Śrī Heruka, who is Mahāmāyā.

The knowledge of that [mantra] is also the Buddha-Ḍākinī Mahāmāyā, because she is of one nature with those two; by means of their applications and ritual acts, such as embracing, kissing, and so forth, one should cause the *yogasamvara*—

Therein, within the interior of the hollow of the pericarp of the navel-lotus, there is a white, subtle drop (*bindu*), which is the yoga, the *saṃvara*,

"Endowed with the five offerings and possessing the five qualities of desire, it is called the 'Siddhi of the Accomplishing Faculty,' which is extremely eternal. One might ask: "Is it only this? To which he replies with the words beginning with "five," meaning that it is accompanied by these ten.

Precisely from that semen of gnosis (*jñānaretas*), having entered the interior of the lotus of the *ḍākinī*, there occurs a gradual radiation of clouds of flowers and so forth, each pervading the sky.

The "qualities of desire" (*kāmaguṇāḥ*) are those things which are both desires and qualities—namely, the sublime forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects. For that is their state of equality.
Therefore, that alone is the place of delight for yogins.

The hero situated in the middle of that is Śrī Heruka.

He becomes the bestower of the great siddhi of the glory of all the Tathāgatas; he constantly acts for the benefit of sentient beings through various types of *rasāyana* (elixirs). Regarding the word *dadāti*: it means "he gives.

"Śrī Sampat.

Regarding "the summoning of *khu ba* (semen), liquor, and the great pill": having summoned the great meat, when one practices together with the Yoginī, one will possess long life, great diligence, great splendor, and great strength; one will be endowed with the divine eye and miraculous powers, drinking [the elixir] day by day and month by month. "Having brought forth" means having drawn out.
"Life" (āyus) is vitality;

"Day by day" means every single day.

"By which it is accomplished... [The phrase] "adorned with three garlands" refers to the abiding state of the joined sun and moon.

that is, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Their "glory" (*śrī*) is their excellence.

"Having drawn [them] in" (*ahrtya*) means having attracted the superknowledge of the eye (*cakṣurabhijñā*). At that time, his lifespan increases and he remains for as long as a great eon (*mahākalpa*); he is never satiated by looking [at them], and he displays emanations of body and miraculous powers. Immediately upon thinking of it in his mind, he completely transforms his own form. Regarding the statement "having a great lifespan" (*mahāyuḥ*), the following passage beginning with "his" (*tasya*) is its explanation.
That yogi would go to, that is, attain, a vast and extensive lifespan;
he is called such because he demonstrates that a great eon (mahākalpa) has its end and limit.
Thus it is said: "the yogi demonstrates."
They are called *pratihārya* because beings are drawn toward (*prati-hriyante*) or led by means of them; the suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), thus forming *pratihārya*.
This is threefold: the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), the miracle of mind-reading (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*), and the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsanī-prātihārya*).

These correspond respectively to the three higher knowledges (*abhijñā*): the power of supernatural transformation (*ṛddhi*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*).
The connection with the preceding clause is: "He displays a body whose form is incomparable, which brings no satiety through repeated sightings.
*Svarūpa* means the essential nature of the self.
“Transformation” (*parivartana*) is the assumption of another form;
it is merely a mental discourse (*manojalpa*) conceived by the mind, such as "May I become like this.
By means of the praise of the Great Miraculous Power of the Sovereign of Knowledge (*vidyeśvarī*), who accomplishes the goal through recitation, he says "Knowledge" (*vidyā*), and so forth.
"Accomplished by recitation" (*pathitasiddhā*) refers to the suffix *kta* used in the present sense; the meaning is that it is accomplished by mere recitation.
Because of her connection with unfailing power, she is "Amoghinī. When she is accomplished, she necessarily bestows the results as described.

"O Vidyā, in the three worlds there is no vidyā equal to mine"—this instruction of all the tantras has been explained to you, O Mother. *Vidye ta iti*: "O Vidyā, there is no other vidyā of mine equal to you."
"In the three worlds" refers to the three families of the Tathāgata-vajra and Padma;
"the scripture" means the sādhana;
"O beautiful one" is an address of invocation.

In the sense of its own object, the suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form] *pratihārya*; [the text reads] *ātmarūpa-stutividye*, etc. Regarding the term *vidya* in the masculine vocative, the presence of a third vocative in the feminine, along with the MMT’s consistent use of *vidyā* as a feminine referent, suggests that both occurrences of *vidya* should be emended to the feminine vocative form *vidye*.

Thus, from the Great Vidyā of the Mistress of Yoginīs (Yogeśvarī), who is my equal, the signs of accomplishment have been shown; this is the first chapter. By means of the aspect of skillful means (upāya) she is the Mistress of Yoginīs (Yogeśvarī), and by means of the aspect of wisdom (prajñā) she is the Great Vidyā; and who is that? She is Mahāmāyā.
Its accomplishment is its performance; its cause is its sign; its various powers are its efficacy; and its exposition is its description.
In the *Guṇavatī*, the commentary on the *Śrīmahāmāyā*, this is the first instruction.

In the *Mahāmāyāṭīkā* (2.1): Now, following that, the excellent secret syllables that bestow the fruit of the accomplishment of the application of the great lordesses of yoginīs shall be explained. Regarding the passage beginning with *atha ataḥ*: this is a single-line verse (*ekapadī-gāthā*) consisting of twelve syllables.
The word *atha* has the sense of introducing the entire recitation (*japa*).

"From this"—meaning after the meditation on the form of the deity—one should contemplate the divine, heroic vessel (*vīrabhājana*) of the Great Yoginīs, which is together with the heroes, as being the pericarp of the navel-lotus; this is the remainder [of the sense].
To the question "What is to be recited therein?", he says "The secret," and so forth.
It is "secret" (guhya) because it is not to be disclosed,
or because by means of it the reality of the deity is concealed; and that which is secret is also the syllable (akṣara).
Yoga is the meditative absorption on the deity;
its accomplishment is its production, which is the fruit; from that very production comes the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā.

Because these two bestow [the goal] with excellence, they grant the fruit of yogic accomplishment (yogasiddhi). Regarding the phrase "merely by thinking" (*cintitamātreṇa*): even without the accomplishment of yoga, merely by reciting [the mantra], one obtains the desired boon, such as the state of a *vidyādhara*. The meaning is that, having seen the secret syllable within the *sampuṭa*, one should raise the Hero (*vīra*) above its head and recite. To the question "How should one recite?", he says: "By the first syllable," and so forth. 2.2 By means of the application of the first syllable, one should always exhale the breath, whereby the supreme Yoginī will be granted merely by being thought of.

Here, the first syllable is the *praṇava*, because it is generally seen at the beginning of mantras; the connection is that the yogi performs [this] by means of its application, that is, by its gradual pronunciation.
What does it do?

It effects the upward movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*). By means of the eighth vowel [Ū] together with the bindu, the yogi performs inhalation, which is free from both existence and non-existence. Now, the divine method for the masters of yoga is demonstrated.
I shall proclaim the secret syllable that bestows the fruit of yogic accomplishment;
by the mere thought of which, the yogins become bestowers of boons.
By employing the first syllable, the yogi always performs inhalation;
joined with the letter *a*, ending with the eighth [vowel], and accompanied by the bindu *u*, he performs exhalation. This is called the "recitation according to one's desire" (*rucijapta*).

How does one produce it?
It is joined with the letter *ū* beneath the letter *ha*, such that it occurs as it is; and at the head of the letter *ha*, it is provided with the bindu, such that it occurs as it is.

The collective meaning is "by means of the syllable *hūṃ*. To the question "What kind of inhalation and exhalation does one perform?", he says: "devoid of existence and non-existence," with the words "respectively" understood as the remainder.
For the meaning of the *praṇava* is pure consciousness alone; the *oṃkāra* is the heart of knowledge, and this is the meaning of the syllable *hūṃ*.
Thus, from the statement in the *Śrī-Guhyasamāja*:

"By means of the reality of the Nirābhāsa," [it follows that] there is equality of body, speech, and mind; and from the statement in that same Tantra: "The syllable HŪṂ brings about the inseparability of the three vajras—body, speech, and mind."

Therefore, because of the vision of the universe—indicated by the syllable *oṃ*—as being mind-only (*cittamātra*), that very universe which is mind-only is "devoid of existence" (*abhāva*), since there is no existence of entities apart from the mind; and because that universe, which is mind-only, attains a state of equality (*samatāpatti*)—that is, becoming free from appearances—that is the syllable *hūṃ*. Through the vision of that, it is "devoid of non-existence."
Thus, it is indicated as being devoid of both existence and non-existence.
Now, what is the nature of the vision of "mind-only" (cittamātratā) and the attainment of equanimity (samatāpatti)?

Herein is the instruction: while pronouncing the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), the Hero (*vīra*) should, along with the exhalation (*ucchvāsa*), behold a line of rays of gnosis (*jñānaraśmi*) rising upward.

Having pervaded [all] with that, one effects the transformation of the universe into the nature of the Buddha while uttering the seed-syllable; then, by visualizing that universe in the form of one's own deity, one perceives it as mind-only.
Thereafter, through the exhalation of the syllable *hūṃ*, one performs the withdrawal of the universe into the Hero (*vīra*) and perceives the attainment of equanimity.
One should perform both of these slowly and repeatedly for as long as no fatigue arises; this is the recitation (*jāpa*) in this tantra.
(2.4) No ascetic observance (*vrata*) has been explained therein.

Even the rites of garlands, mantras, dhāraṇīs, and fire offerings will cease one after another. Here, he explains the ease of practice for that [mantra] with the words beginning "na tasya" and so forth. "Tasya" refers to the one who recites [the mantra].
"Vrata" refers to the observances such as silence, bathing, and begging for alms.

Because of non-existence, it is indicated by the syllable *hūṃ*; it is devoid of both existence and non-existence.
