And the meaning "delight" (*ram*) is also understood.

Apart from these, there is also what is called the threefold application consisting of mantra, form, and dharma; indeed, one is not defiled by the faults of existence through the three types of gnosis.
Now, as for *japa*—is it merely verbal recitation that must be performed here, or is there also the cultivation of the knowledge of the [deity's] form? To this, he says: "Mantra," and so forth.
Yoga is meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that has reality as its object.
That yoga is threefold, of three types. Why?
Because he is of the nature of the dharma consisting of mantra and form:
mantra is speech that illuminates reality;
form is the embodiment of the deity.
Knowledge of the meaning of the mantra is *dharma*.

By means of the threefold knowledge—by the three yogas just mentioned, and not by mere verbal discourse—one shall not be defiled by the faults of existence; that is to say, one is liberated from the defects of *saṃsāra*, such as evil and so forth.
In this way, through constant practice by the yogin, even the state equal to Vajrasattva will be accomplished in one month. Thus is the triad of *evam* yogas.
"Constantly" (*nityam*) means every day;
"continually" (*satatam*) means at each junction of the day (*pratisandhyam*).
"Siddhyata" means "is accomplished.
Vajrasattva is Śrī Heruka. "Equal to him" means similar to him.
By the word "also," he is equal to Vajraḍākinī.
"He" refers to the yogin.
Therefore, in this context, the form of Heruka and the ḍākinīs should be meditated upon with the sense of identity (*tad-ahaṃkāra*).
The mantra consists of the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and the syllable *hūṃ*, which are uttered slowly, and within them, the root mantra is also uttered slowly.

Regarding the knowledge of the meaning of the mantra: having raised the *vīrabindu* at the head of the letters of the *vidyā* situated within the cavity formed by the union of the sun and moon, one should effect the transformation of all phenomena into the nature of the Buddha by means of the ray of light arising from it;
furthermore, their withdrawal into the *vīrabindu* is to be understood.

Thus, when the recitation has been performed for six months through the methods of mantra, form, and dharma, whether or not a corresponding accomplishment (*siddhi*) has been attained, the syllables of the *vidyā*—when correctly applied—will necessarily accomplish the ritual action according to its own nature. One should meditate on the first syllable as possessing the color of Indra; if one applies it to one's own *vidyā*, it will summon [the deity] instantly. Therefore, in order to indicate the syllables of the *vidyā* and their applications, he says "Indravarṇa," and so forth.

The *indragopa* is the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that takes reality as its object; it should be understood by the yogi through threefold knowledge. Having raised up the knowledge of the meaning of the *dākinīs'* mantra at the head, it is to be known whether it has been attained or not attained. It is expressed by the word "Indra. The first syllable is the *praṇava*.
One should apply the meditation upon it for the sake of attraction.
"One who possesses knowledge is a *vidyā-yogī*.
That yogi brings that object of meditation quickly.
'Quickly' is explained as 'in an instant (*kṣaṇāt*')."

This is what is meant: having performed the yoga of the Buddha-Ḍākinī and so forth, and having visualized the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) as reddish-saffron in a hero’s vessel (*vīrabhājana*), one should place the Hero within its drop (*bindu*). Having rendered the Hero reddish by means of the rays of the *praṇava*, one should emanate two lines of reddish rays from the Hero; at the tip of one, one should visualize a noose, and at the tip of the second, a hook (*aṅkuśa*).
One should contemplate the person to be subdued (*sādhya*) bound by the noose around the neck and pierced in the heart by the hook, being swiftly drawn forth.
Within a moment, he becomes drawn forth.

If one contemplates and meditates upon that which is endowed with the second syllable, all three stages without exception will come under one's control. *Tīyam* is the letter *Ā*; "endowed with that" refers to the second [syllable] and so forth. In the *Āli-pāṭha*, that which is raised up as the second is the Hero (*vīra*).
By means of that, the supreme beings—the yogins—meditate and delight their own deity.
"Vibhāvana" means the cultivation of various things to be accomplished (*sādhyabhāvana*). "All" refers to those things to be accomplished.
"Entirely" is understood to have the sense of "even all."
It brings even the entire triple world under its control;
how much more so a hundred beings or a thousand beings—this is the meaning. What has been stated?

Having made the form of any one of the six [deities] red as the *japā* flower, and having placed that red-as-*japā* form within a casket, one should place a hero, likewise colored by that same [red], upon its top.

Having caused the object of the rite (*sādhya*) to be colored down to every single atom by means of its rays, one should visualize them as being brought under control and falling at one's feet, thinking:
"May they all come under my power."
When Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and likewise Īśvara and Kāmeśvara are impelled by the syllable of primordial wisdom (jñānākṣara), they are summoned together with their consorts (*bhāryā*).
These—Brahmā and the others—are drawn forth.
Because it is imperishable (*akṣaya*), the "syllable" (*akṣara*) is the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*).
Its secret syllable is the syllable beyond syllables (*akṣarākṣara*).
In some places it is called "knowledge of the syllable" (*akṣarajñāna*);
there, "knowledge" means the seed-syllable, the *hūṃ* residing in both [the upper and lower parts], and that, when drawn forth, is red as a hibiscus flower.
Impelled by those rays, Virād, having been summoned by Aruṇaraśmi,
was thus joined [to him].
[atom by atom] [one's own deity] [various]
"Whatever is desired" refers to those who are to be converted (*sādhyāḥ*).
"All of them" refers to those who are to be proven.
The aggregate of the six [atoms].
The supreme atom.
These [syllables] are drawn forth when they have been impelled by the seed-syllable.
How are they impelled?
Like the practice of the first extraction (*ākṛṣṭi*).
Others say that here the extraction is by means of the syllable *hūṃ* and by exhalation.
In this tantra, some say that the "applications for all types of summoning" refer to the trunks of light rays arising from the Hero.

Regarding the phrase "perfectly endowed with the letter A," it means that if one meditates on the three applications well-established in body, speech, and mind, it is the supreme summoning of the *piṇḍa* (the mass). He explains the supreme summoning of the *piṇḍa* with the words beginning with "in the form of A.
"Endowed with those two" refers to the letter A and the syllable [HŪṂ]; the meaning is that the practitioners are perfectly joined with the letter A or with the syllable HŪṂ.
"Threefold conjunction" (*trisamyoga*) means a conjunction consisting of three [factors].
"Established in body, speech, and mind" means that it is situated in the body, the throat, and the heart of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
What is being stated?

Having made one of the six [syllables] swift and reddish-brown, and having placed the Hero upon the head of the letter *Ā* or within the dot (*bindu*) of the syllable *HŪṂ* inside the hollow interior of the *saṃpuṭa*, one should visualize the victim—arisen from the wind-maṇḍala produced from the syllable *YAM*—mounted upon it. Having bound him by the neck with two cords and pierced him in the heart by means of two lines of rays, red like a hero, and being drawn through the atmosphere, one should contemplate him as being swiftly dragged away.
In an instant, he is summoned.

"Endowed with the syllable *khe*, red in color, four-faced, and holding a skull and a noose in his hands—he is the supreme for summoning the seminal essence (*śukra*). Regarding *khekāre* and so forth, this is what is meant:

having visualized oneself as white, four-faced, holding a skull and a noose in one's hands, and possessing a red mind, one should imagine that by means of a tube of light rays arising from the hero situated at the head of the syllable *khe*, one enters the secret place of the object of practice and draws forth their seminal essence into the skull; one should contemplate it being performed there.
In an instant, it becomes summoned.

The syllable *ci* is endowed with a medicinal essence; it is yellow in color and has a universal radiance. Having visualized the form of a horse’s face, one should contemplate the syllable *ci*: by means of the trunk of the heroic light-rays situated upon the head of the syllable *ci*, one draws up the liquor contained within the vessel and should imagine the vessel being filled.
In an instant, it becomes full. [Thus it is drawn.]
[It is] situated at the [point of] attraction of the six.
The syllable Khe,
red in color, born from the syllable Yam.
The noose [is] the self [the medicine].

If one meditates with a wrathful mind upon [the syllable] *yi*, which is yellow in color and perfectly endowed with the letter *ra*—red in hue, possessing great radiance, four-armed, four-faced, and well-situated in the form of a jackal (*jambuka*)—this is the supreme method for summoning blood. Regarding the phrase "with *rakāra*" and so forth: by means of the letter *ra*, one should visualize oneself as red in color, four-armed, four-faced, with the face of a jackal, and of great brilliance; being wrathful, one should contemplate that blood is being drawn from the body of the target by a ray of light resembling a leech, just as described previously.

One should perform the definitive placement (*nyāsa*) of the six syllables upon the six locations. This is the yoga of the assembly of Yoginīs and Vajrayoginīs; it is the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) of these very syllables of the *vidyā* upon the two eyes, the ears, and so forth, through union with one’s own deity (*svadevatāyoga*).
Therefore, in this context, he speaks of that [placement] as well, beginning with the words "six," and so on.
The "six" refers to the six syllables of the *vidyā* mentioned immediately above; the connection is that [the practice] is conjoined with those six phonemes.
The remainder [of the sentence] is "the body of one's own deity.
To the question "Wherein is it joined?", he says: "In six locations," which means in six places.
This being so, the Vajrayoginīs are accomplished, and not otherwise.
Vajra is Heruka;
the yoginīs are the five ḍākinīs;
yoga is Śrī Heruka.
His consort is the ḍākinī.
In the *Saṃvara*, it is stated that when there is supreme bliss together with those very same yoginīs, [it occurs] in six locations.
He states those very locations, and no others, beginning with "the eyes" and so forth.
*Mānasa* means the heart.

By the word "and" (*ca*), the tongue and the body are also included. With the *siṃhavikrīḍita-mudrā*, the yogi should cause [the vital energy] to remain; having restrained the breath and effort (*prāṇāyāma*), if one meditates, at that very moment it blazes. Reaching the end of existence in Akaniṣṭha, the seven worlds of the moving and the non-moving—the *Yogāntara* says, beginning with "Lion" (*siṃha*) and so forth.
"Simha" means a hero.
That [mudrā] in which his playful sport occurs is so described.
"Mudrā" refers to the union of the sun and the moon.
"Bind" means they contemplate [the victim] as bound by three rows of syllables, as previously described.
*Jambuka* (C: *jambu*). "Enraged" (B: *kraddham*). "Lightning-leeches" (T: *srin po padma'i gzugs can*, "a demon in the form of a lotus").
Purified; Mp: [referring to] the self.
Immediately after; B: emends *antaro* in a marginal note.
One should contemplate; T: should be applied with certainty.
T begins this line with *yang na*.
Regarding *dākinī*, C provides the editorial emendation to *ḍākinīgaṇaḥ*.
Regarding *sukhavare*, T translates it as *spyod pa las byung ba'i bde ba'i mchog* (the supreme bliss arising from conduct).
*rnam rol* (M) / *rnal 'byor* (Mp): by means of yoga.
*yogina iti*: those who abide in the yoga of Śrī Heruka, surrounded by the four goddesses.
"Prāṇāyāma" refers to inhalation and exhalation. "Well-restrained" means having properly restrained them by gradually making them subtle.
"Having meditated" means having fixed the mind upon that very hero, who is visible through the opening of the moon's aperture (the *brahmarandhra*).
"It blazes at that very moment" means that for one whose mind is stabilized upon the Hero (Vīra), knowledge blazes forth instantly; it produces a flash of light (*jvālābhāsa*).
To what distance does it blaze? He says: "the seven worlds.
These are the seven worlds: the netherworld (*pātāla*), the earth, heaven, and the first, second, third, and fourth meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
The collective aggregate of these is "the seven worlds" (saptaloka), which is neuter, like the term "the three worlds" (tribhuvana).
The first three dhyānas each consist of three stages,
while the fourth consists of eight stages.
Its eighth stage is Akaniṣṭha;
therefore it is called "having the Akaniṣṭha world as its limit," and therein dwell sentient beings.
Immobile things are the celestial palaces, abodes, and so forth; mobile things are [beings]. Therefore, it is called "the mobile and the immobile.

Although everyone meditates upon that, it is not realized by them. If all were to realize it perfectly, the play of worldly existence would be destroyed; therefore, this gnosis is secret, unmanifest, and without letters.
And in order to demonstrate that state of invisibility, he says "cultivating" and so forth;
"all" means all sentient beings;
"cultivating" means practicing repeatedly, because they perceive their own minds in various such ways.
And they do not perceive it as such, because it appears to the foolish through unreal forms;

thus, the world is a play. The destruction of the conceptualization of duality through those various appearances would have already occurred previously, for the world-play would have perished long ago.
And since it has not perished even until now, therefore this knowledge— the reality of knowledge— is non-dual and beyond the reach of heroes.
It is hidden from the ignorant; by whom was it concealed through delusions that manifest unreal forms?
Of what nature is it?
Because it is beyond the range of speech, it is unmanifest;
because it is not an object of mental verbalization, it is without syllables.
Because the Buddhas, possessing the yoga of gnosis and being perfectly endowed with sleep, meditate upon that mind which has become a single sphere as a single form—
[the text] says "they perceive" (*buddhayanti*) and so forth;
the word *hi* is used for emphasis, and *jñāna* refers to the flame of primordial wisdom (*ye shes kyi me lce*).
The neuter [form] is *tribhuvana* (the three worlds); *om acarā* refers to immovable things such as celestial palaces (*vimāna*) and abodes (*bhavana*),
while *sacārācara* (or *carācara*) refers to both the moving and the immovable.
By that... [it is said]:
"Oṃ! May it be seen and not seen by all sentient beings"—that is, may this appear as it does to all sentient beings.
"Of all" means "of all sentient beings"; that is, all sentient beings.
"Known by all" means [known] by all sentient beings.
"By means of the unreal" (abhūtaiḥ) [means] because of not seeing reality (tattva).

"It perishes" (vinaśyati): if it were perceived by everyone, the play of worldly existence would have perished from the very beginning; however, such has not been the case up to the present. Because it is so, it is said: "this gnosis is secret."
Of what kind [is it]? And the reversal of the word order is as follows: "the perfectly awakened ones" (sambuddhāḥ) means "the Tathāgatas" (tathāgatāḥ).
If that vision were established by nature even for the Tathāgatas, then there would be no possibility of others attaining it.
Now, if that [state] were dependent on yoga, then others too would perceive it through that very same yoga; therefore, he says "by yoga," etc.
Because it possesses the common characteristic of sleep due to its state of absolute non-distraction, it is "yoga-sleep" (*yoganidrā*), being both yoga and sleep.
Having come together with her, being thus united, they meditate upon his very instructions— namely,
all phenomena (sarvadharma) in the form of "thusness" (tathatā) and so forth.

"One" refers to the "mass" (*piṇḍa*), which is of a single flavor consisting solely of luminosity devoid of appearances; because those very [appearances] are completely condensed and rendered extremely subtle, it is the "mass," which is merely a drop (*bindu*) as fine as a mustard seed—
this establishes the form of the Hero's consort (*mudrā*).
"With minds directed toward that" means that the mind is fixed precisely upon that physical body (*piṇḍa*);
by this, the meaning of "yoga-sleep" is indicated.

Having meditated on whatever arises from the nine gates as being of the nature of substance, one should eat with a non-conceptual mind possessed of the realization of selflessness. With the words beginning "They meditate," he states the *samaya*, which is the cause for the accomplishment of such yogas.
"To cultivate" means "to resolve with conviction. What should one resolve upon?
Those objects which arise from the [four] doors of speech.
The meaning is: one should resolve that the Buddhas are of the nature of Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, and Amoghasiddhi—eternal and of an unerring nature;
one should "consume" them for the purpose of consuming conceptual constructions.
"Without conceptualization" (*nirvikalpena*) means without doubt;
"without intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvena*) means without the appearance of the grasped and the grasper;
"by the wise one" (*dhīmatā*) means by a mind that culminates in mere luminosity—this is the remainder [of the meaning].

"By means of the thumb and the ring finger, one will attain the eternal siddhi arising from the nature of nectar within the mouth of the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). Regarding "thumb" and so forth: the meaning is that the wish-fulfilling gem is situated in the mouth of the thumb and the ring finger; the implication is that one should then consume those very [substances] with that [gem].
When? He says: "from nectar," and so forth.

The meaning is: when all that has become of the nature of nectar according to the method to be described, what would then happen? To this he says, "Siddhim," and so forth. Yoga-adhinam: yoga is both this [state] and sleep; these are the forms, and thus one should have conviction (*adhimuñcet*)—the wise one should have conviction—in all phenomena as being of the nature of the Buddha. Regarding "thumb" and so forth, and "siddhim" and so forth: this is the second chapter, the determination of the application, from the Great Vidyā of the Mistress of Yoginīs (*Yoginīśvarī-mahāvidyā*).
It has been explained that she is the Great Vidyā, the Mistress of Yoga (Yogeśvarī).

Her yoga is the union of the sun and moon, which is the union of the *bindu*. The manner in which that is determined by means of the "Lion's Play" (*siṃhavikrīḍitā*) and so forth is its definitive exposition (*nirṇaya*).
Its exposition—

the second exposition in the *Mahāmāyā-ṭīkā* entitled *Guṇavatī*— is as follows: "Now, that which is to be correctly explained is the supreme accomplishment of the commitments (*samaya-sādhana*), the collection of other substances to be consumed, which bestows the fruit of omniscience."
"Others" refers to those different from the nine just mentioned;
they are both substances (*dravya*) and groups (*gaṇa*),
because each constitutes a portion of a group— thus they are called "substance-groups" (*dravyagaṇa*).
"Omniscient" means omniscience; that itself is the fruit.

To those who bestow it, by merely consuming [it], the Mothers of the Bhūtas are accomplished. Likewise, being endowed with stability and swift movement, as well as with a bull and a great dog, one partakes of the five nectars of gnosis through the collection of substances.

Having prepared a mixture of *bhūtamātṛ* and *mahāpalala* together with the great *vajraḍākinīs*, one should place it in the center of a *ce-spyang* (a ritual vessel) for seven days. Then, having extracted it and formed pills the size of a fruit, this is what is taught in this tantra. However, for eight or fourteen days, one should meditate on them together for seven days, prepare the mixture, and place it in the center of a *ce-spyang*. Having extracted it from that, from the five [elements], [it is called] "Omniscient" (*sarvajña*). Child!

"O Mothers of Beings! [This is] a great mass of meat. Regarding "in the collection" (*samuccaye*), one should make pills the size of a fruit of accomplishment (*siddhi-phala*). As for "on the fourteenth day" (*caturdaśī*) and so forth: here, the short vowel in *aṣṭamī* and the long vowel in *jambūka* are Vedic (*chāndasa*). Having meditated on each individually with the words "along with" (*asaha*), and having made them smeared and dried with nectar, [one should proceed] for seven days, beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.

"In the middle of the *śivāṅga*"—having done thus, one should subsequently "apply them," that is, having unified them; "on a night of the elements" (bhūtarātrau) they are "to be established" (*sthāpanīya*).
"Those things to be established" (*sthāpanīyāni*) refers to those substances (*dravyāṇi*) which have been meditated upon and established in such a manner.
"Siddhārtha fruits" means [fruits] the size of mustard seeds; as for what those "vyānis" are, he says "five," meaning five palas.
Likewise, because the term "measure" (*pramāṇa*) is used as an illustration, it refers to such a configuration.

"Because the great fruit is thoroughly realized, it is spoken of in this tantra as 'completely hidden'; the great fruit has been hidden everywhere by the Buddha. Since it was stated "it is spoken of in this tantra," it means it was stated in its entirety;
for this very reason, he says, "and in other tantras," and so forth.
Having asked, "Having done what is it hidden? he replies: "Because of attaining a state of similarity with the Heroes (vīra)."
Thus, not everything has been said;
to the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"Having understood them to be 'attachment' and 'the past,' they are of great fruit"—that is to say, having known that they are of great fruit.
From what [source] do the great fruits arise?

The *Sādhanasambhava* (Arising of the Sādhana) from the *Śivāṅga* [section] concerning the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) which have been transformed into the five wisdoms (*pañcajñāna*). One should mentally visualize a lotus, red in color and all-pervadingly radiant, perfectly endowed with the four goddesses and adorned with the forms of the Buddhas. Having meditated upon it and prepared the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one should place it together for seven days, beginning on the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight. Here, the entire procedure has been stated; therefore, knowing that it is well-guarded, one should understand the great fruits for those who abide in the limbs of Śiva. "Then," and so forth.

The word *atha* means "immediately following. In this tantra, that by which the Blessed One together with his maṇḍala is accomplished—that is, propitiated—is the *sādhana*; the meaning is that one should practice it.

One should visualize a lotus through the meditation on the non-manifest bodhicitta, having made the world equal to space. Having contemplated the ground as consisting of vajras, one should contemplate within the interior of a peaked pavilion situated in the midst of eight formidable cremation grounds a [lotus] with eight petals or four petals, possessing a uniform red color and red luster—meaning it is both red and has a red radiance.

Having mentally— by means of the drop of the perfectly pure mind (manas) known as Vīra, which is situated at the pericarp and radiates forth— perceived [the mandala] as joined with the four goddesses stationed on the petals in the four directions, and when there is the radiation from each of the drops on the eastern petal and so forth of the lords of the Vajra, Maṇi, Padma, and Karma families, as well as their respective infinite families; then, by those Vajra, Ratna, Padma, and Viśva-Ḍākinīs produced from that reabsorption, it is occupied upon those very petals and adorned with the images of the Buddhas.
Buddha is Vajradhara;
his image or form is Śrī Heruka, by whom— the leader of the maṇḍala— it is adorned.

By those very goddesses, through the impulsion of the song to be described, from the root mind-bindu transformed into the form of the two seed-syllables, the five families and their lords emanate, pervading all directions; then, through the dissolution and the re-expansion of those two seed-syllables, the Blessed Śrī Heruka, embraced by Buddha-Ḍākinī, [adorns the mandala].

In the east is blue light like that of an *utpala* flower; in the south, yellow; in the west, white and red light; and in the north, variegated light. It is entwined with garlands of blazing flames, and is beautiful with four faces, four arms, and three eyes. Furthermore, as to what the form of the Buddha-image is like, he says "in the east," and so forth.
"Four-faced, four-armed, and three-eyed" is easy to understand.

He explains what color each face has: the eastern face is the color of a blue lotus, the southern face is yellow, and the western face is white. That which is the means of accomplishment (sādhana) is that by which the ritual action is performed; thus, one should perform that [action]. Having emanated the intermediate space, and so forth, with the mind in the four [directions]... it is observed that, upon the emanation of those banks, it is adorned by the transformation of the two seed-syllables through the emanation of those banks and the transformation of the two seed-syllables. "Red" refers to the four faces; "white" means that the upper face is the color of a ruby (marakata).
It is well known that whatever color is at the opening of the root [channel], that same color is on the body.
"Filled with garlands of flames" means that it is so described because it is crowded with garlands of flames blazing intensely during the dissolution [process].
One should visualize the goddess of the eastern direction as having three eyes; in her left hands she holds a *khatvāṅga* and a bell, and in her right hands she holds a vajra and a skull-cup.
The goddess of the southern direction holds in her hands a trident, a jewel, a banner, and a *ce-sbyang*.
The goddess of the western direction holds in her hands a bow, an arrow, a variegated lotus, and a skull-cup.
The goddess of the northern direction holds in her hands a sword, a noose, a small drum (*ḍamaru*), and a skull-cup.
With the words beginning with "on the left" (vāme), he describes the emblems of the goddesses: "she has a khaṭvāṅga and a bell on the left" means she holds a khaṭvāṅga and a bell in her left hands;
"likewise, with a vajra and a skull-cup in her right hands" means she holds both a vajra and a skull-cup in her two right hands—thus she is so described.
"In the east" means on the eastern petal;
the phrase "the goddess" is to be connected everywhere in all subsequent instances as well;
here, for now, it refers to Vajraḍākinī.
In the subsequent [section], they are respectively Ratnaḍākinī, Padmaḍākinī, and Viśvaḍākinī;
and "in the south," and so forth. She is so described because she holds in her hands a trident, a jewel, a banner, and a jackal.
The word "in the west" (paścimena) is used in the instrumental case with the sense of the locative.
Because she possesses a bow, an arrow, a universal lotus, and a skull-cup, she is called *Dhanurbāṇaviśvapadmakapālinī*.
Regarding the term *Khaḍgetyādi*: she has a sword, a noose, a hand-drum, and a skull-cup in her hands; thus she is so described.
These [attendant goddesses] also have garlands of flames, four faces, four arms, and three eyes; for subordinate qualities follow the nature of the principal one.
Therefore, according to the face of the Bhagavān, their eastern face is blue, the southern yellow, the western white, and the northern dark; their faces are likewise,
but the root face of these [goddesses] has the color of their bodies,
and in place of the body-colored face of the Bhagavān, they have a blue face.

"One should visualize the vajras of body, speech, and mind in its center"—that is, the skull-cup (*kapāla*), the *khatvāṅga*, as well as the bow and arrow. By the words "body," and so forth, he states the locations and emblems of the Bhagavān:
"The Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind" refers to Śrī Heruka;
one should contemplate him.
"In that [place]" means in the center of the red lotus; "in the pericarp" (*karṇikāyām*); "a skull," etc.—the remainder [of the sentence] is "in his hands."
Just as Śrī Heruka is, so too is Buddhaḍākinī; however, she is red in color and has a red face at the base, and she faces him with her two arms firmly embracing his neck.

If one meditates while being perfectly endowed with the initial mantra, it blazes up at that very moment. Thus, when practiced by a yogin, it bestows the supreme reality of substances. Regarding the phrase *teṣvasyā*, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative; through its connection [with the mantra], [one attains] the Skull-Bearer (*kapālinī*). She has a face with garlands of flames and is white in color. Since there are no accomplishments without the pledge (*samaya*), he says "Ādi," and so forth, in order to explain the kindling of the pledge.
The "initial mantra" is the *praṇava* (Oṃ); the connection is that the pledge-substance blazes when joined with that.
"Having meditated" means that when one has meditated according to the instruction,
"the substance" refers to the *samaya*-substance;
"accomplishing" means he brings it to completion.
What kind [of result] does it accomplish that bestows the fruit of accomplishment?
And it is said in the glorious *Guhyasamāja*: "Having meditated upon the syllable Oṃ of all mantras, one blazes forth at that very moment. Thus it is said.

Through the ritual application for the accomplishment of the Yoginīs, there arises immediate conviction; it is not seen by anyone, yet it appears as a thousandfold radiance. Regarding the benefits of the blazing [flame], it says "yoga" and so forth: here, the world develops the conviction that there exist yogas belonging to yogins—that is, yogins and yoginīs who have attained accomplishment—based on the example of their radiant power. *Jvālanānuśaṃsā*. It says "yoga" and so forth. Here, the conviction of the world proceeds that there truly exist yogas of the yogins—that is, yogins and yoginīs who are accomplished (*siddha*). This is due to the example of their majestic splendor. *Jvāla* (B9b).
The meaning is "the vision of the response.
By the words beginning with "antar," he describes his power (*prabhāva*), such as the attainment of invisibility and so forth.
"Illuminating a single thousandfold world" means that a thousand world-systems consisting of four continents is a "thousandfold world-system" (*sāhasro lokadhātuḥ*).

The illuminator of that single [reality] through its sovereignty and its activity for the sake of others, having surpassed all Buddhas, enjoys the most excellent divine maidens; he beholds with vajra-eyes the Buddhas themselves, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, residing in the vajra-abode, like a myrobalan fruit held in the palm of his hand. The phrase "of all the siddhas" should be construed with "the maiden," referring to those such as the Vidyādharas.
The adamantine abode is the buddha-field established for those very Buddhas; together with their assemblies, it is established as that very adamantine abode.
Thus, [he visualizes] those established in the adamantine abode.
“Eye-vajra” (*cakṣurvajra*) means the vajra-eye, which is to say the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*).
“In his own hand,” and so forth, means just as a single *āmalaka* fruit rests in one’s own hand.

“Even fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges”—this refers to the Buddha-fields; the meaning is that he knows the beings residing therein, who possess the nature and characteristics of body, speech, and mind, and who arise from the dance of the mind, being the essence of all things.

Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of body, speech, and mind": their characteristics are as follows; the bodies and minds are the sensory cognitions (*indriyajñāna*), while speech and mind are the mental cognitions (*manovijñāna*). Because they are accompanied by discursive thought (*sajalpatva*), they cultivate their own nature; thus, they "see" with the mind.
How do they see?
The meaning is "by means of the universal self as the universal self.
To the question "What is this? What is this? he says: "Mind," and so forth.
"Called mind" means the vajra-mind, which is the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) of knowing the minds of others.
In Yoga Tantra, the meditation on oneself in the form of one's own deity is called "the drama" (*nāṭaka*) here, because of its similarity to a drama.
Therefore, it is so described because its arising [occurs] from that.

In the practice of the *samaya* substances, a little has been said; now [the following] is taught. By means of the arrangement of reversed syllables, one should visualize the mantra there. Fully endowed with vajra-water, one should consume each pill. That which is joined at the end with the eight syllables, together with the vowel *ū* and the bindu, should be uttered as the mantra: *guhyabhakṣa abhakṣe hūṃ*. Through the union with all the yoginīs, fully endowed with the first syllable—if the Vajradhara desires accomplishment—the yogin should consume it seven times after consecrating it. It is called "the end of the three syllables," well-situated at the end of the eight. Together with the vowel *ū* and the bindu, it is the supreme syllable, the locus of the mind of all sentient beings, arising from the drama.

The meaning is that one possesses the superknowledge (*abhijñā*) of knowing the minds of others in their entirety. Regarding the drama (*nāṭaka*), because of its similarity to a drama, it is "brief" (*stokam*). One should apply the syllable *hrīḥ* at the beginning; one should apply it correctly at the end of the syllables. One should fill [the space] with the five seed-syllables and meditate upon them with the letters so as to cause the lotus to fully blossom. If one desires the accomplishment of the Vajra-holder, one should understand all such applications. Then, here, the intention of the Vajrayoginīs is taken up through the Glorious Vajra Song, which thoroughly accomplishes existence: "O Friend! O Vajra, you who awaken by opening the lotus—*Alala ho!* May you be thoroughly pleased by the dance of Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*)! With the light of the Mother, the mouth of the lotus is fully opened; may you be thoroughly pleased by the dance of Great Bliss! To the Great Vajra-holder! Then, here, merely by singing this song, the Vajra-ḍākinīs perform a dance that perfectly exhorts Vajrasattva. Thus, for one who is always possessed of devotion, the accomplishment of the application (*yogasiddhi*) will occur. Through application during the four periods of the day, accomplishment will be attained. With the supreme ornament of meditation complete in every way, adorned with perfumes and flowers, one will certainly obtain the accomplishment that bestows the supreme three bodies (*trikāya*). This [light] shines forth over an extent of a hundred *yojanas*. *Alala ho! Mahāsukheṇa ārohiu ṇacceng!* (O Great Bliss, ascend and dance!)
The lotus has blossomed through the rays of the sun; with great bliss!
A-la-la-la-la-ho! With great bliss, he has ascended and dances.

By the thorough union of the two organs, the unsurpassed reality (tattva) of the peaceful state—the awakening of the Buddhas—arises from the nine gates as a substance and is accomplished. {541.17} Even for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, such peace exists.
Thereupon, he specifies [the term] "reality" (*tattva*), meaning knowledge devoid of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Such knowledge also exists for Bodhisattvas, yet it is surpassed by the knowledge of a Buddha.
Therefore, for the sake of distinction, he says "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
"Anuttara" (unexcelled) means that there is nothing superior to this.

Here, the verse (*śloka*) is a summary verse regarding the meaning of the tantra as it has been explained: "Forms, likewise mudrās, signs, and substances; the various methods of the ritual for meditating on the different dhyānas; and the goddesses who inspire desire have been taught.
In this context, *rūpaṇī* refers to the colors and physical forms of the deities and so forth.

"Mudrās" refers to the sealings (*mudraṇāni*), such as the sixfold placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and the purification of the lotus (*śābjaśodhana*) and so forth. "Its very symbols" refers to the skull-bowl, the *khaṭvāṅga* staff, and so forth. "Substances" refers to the objects of the pledge (*samayavastu*).
"Meditations" (*dhyānāni*) means "meditations" (*dhyai*), which signifies "contemplation" (*cintā*); that is, the recitations (*japa*).
"Cultivations" (*bhāvanāni*) refers to the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) such as the mandala-circle and so forth.
"Various methods" (*nānāvidhā upāyāḥ*) refers to the accomplishment of activities through the expansion of ritual actions and so forth.
All these have been demonstrated and indicated.
To the question of what has been accomplished by all this, he says: "The goddess," and so forth.
Whatever was desired by the mind, whatever was desired by the heart of the goddess Mahāmāyā, those things have been stated.

In whosever house this tantra resides, and who constantly upholds, recites, and meditates upon it—for that person no diseases shall arise, nor shall there be old age or obstacles, and they shall not die; rather, they will be constantly and at all times protected and guarded by the wealthy yoginīs. Regarding the benefits of upholding the tantra, he says with the verse beginning "the tantra," etc.:
"tantra" refers to the one called *Mahāmāyā*.
"In whose house" means in the house of whichever [person].
"Bhavan nityam" means "one should remain constantly.
"Dhārayet" means "one should maintain [it].
"Vācayet" means "one should cause [others] to recite"; the meaning is that one should read it aloud.
"One should contemplate" means one should visualize. "Obstacles" refers to hindrances.

This is the third chapter, the *sādhana* (accomplishment method) together with the ritual application (*upacāra*), which is the supreme secret and great secret of the intention of the Great Vajrayoginīs. [The term *śodhana* is rendered as "application" (*sbyor ba*) in the Tibetan.]
[The passage beginning with] "devī ye" etc., [is read as] "devītyādi" in K and C;
"mahāmāyāyāḥ" in C is "mahāmayayā";
and "tiṣṭeta" in K and C is "tistate."
"Vibhāvayitā" means one should cultivate [the visualization].
"The Great Vajraḍākinīs" refers to those [deities];
their doctrine—that is, the tenet embraced by them—is the entire Yoginītantra; such is the meaning.
Its secret is its essence.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "The great secret.
At the beginning [of the *Jābāla-upaniṣad*], it was called the "supreme secret."
(543) At the end, that very same "Great Secret" is stated by another synonym; the meaning is that it is the tantra known as Mahāmāyā. That is completed and finalized.
"With its ritual application" (*sopacāram*) means that the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) for the sake of the goal and the means is the application (*upacāra*).
"It exists together with that" means "it is accompanied by it," which is to say, "it is not empty of it.
Whatever merit I have acquired by composing this commentary on the *Mahāmāyā-tantra*, may that merit, having reached the fullness of the moon, become radiant.

May I alone attain the state of a Victor, the nature of the Vajra-holder; and may all the world thereafter obtain the absolute destruction of suffering. Thus ends the third instruction in the *Mahāmāyā-ṭīkā*, which possesses all virtues.
The commentary on the *Mahāmāyā* entitled *Guṇavatī*, by the scholar Paṇḍita Ratnākaraśāntipāda, is completed. It was composed under his patronage. (K:
*utparigṛhītaḥ*; C: *uparigṛhītaḥ*).
[Regarding the term *paryāya*, B emends it to *paryāntareṇa* in a marginal note.]
This is the meaning. [T:
om *avāptam*] K: having attained; C:
possessing the luster of the full moon.

That source of precious jewels, the entire world, has been definitively blessed by the Perfect Buddhas and their Sons; thus, the activities of his body, speech, and mind are for the sake of benefiting migratory beings.

This commentary on the difficult points of the supreme tantra called *Mahāmāyā*, which joins the white [text] with the realization of words and meaning, is endowed with qualities and attracts the hearts of people like a string of pearls.
